analysis.one_liner: Sets a national net-zero emissions goal and requires electric suppliers to reach 100% zero-emission power by 2035.
analysis.headline: A comprehensive Democratic climate bill with 21 cosponsors never received a committee vote or a House floor vote in nearly two years; the only action was one subcommittee hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: The CLEAN Future Act was a sweeping climate bill: it set national goals to cut greenhouse gas emissions 50% below 2005 levels by 2030 and reach net-zero by 2050, and required electricity suppliers to deliver an ever-larger share of zero-emission power, reaching 100% by 2035, with a system of tradable clean-energy credits. It bundled in building efficiency rebates, electric vehicle programs, worker transition aid, environmental justice grants, methane limits on oil and gas operations, and a requirement that clean-energy construction pay prevailing wages. It was referred to 11 House committees in March 2021 and never came out of any of them.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to climate change and air pollution, since the bill's core is an economywide emissions reduction mandate. Low- and moderate-income households get heating assistance, home retrofit rebates, solar grants, and electric-vehicle access programs. Construction and energy workers get prevailing-wage guarantees and union-friendly conditions attached to clean-energy credits. Communities living near polluting facilities get air monitoring, cleanup funds, and new rights to technical help. Emerging industries — solar, wind, nuclear, storage, EV manufacturing — get guaranteed demand, credits, and federal grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, clean energy workers, and fenceline communities

how_it_helps.text: Sets a national interim goal of at least a 50% cut in greenhouse gas emissions from 2005 levels by 2030 and a net-zero-by-2050 goal, and requires every federal agency to write a plan to meet them.

Requires retail electricity suppliers to provide a rising share of zero-emission electricity starting in 2023, reaching 100% by 2035, backed by a credit trading program and civil penalties for noncompliance.

Bars issuance of clean-electricity credits unless prevailing wages were paid on construction, and requires generator owners to stay neutral toward union organizing as a condition of receiving credits.

Directs help toward households with the least room to absorb the transition: reauthorized low-income energy assistance (LIHEAP), solar grants for low-income and underserved areas, retrofit rebates with special terms for moderate-income households, and EV access programs for underserved communities.

Creates environmental justice programs — technical assistance grants, air toxics monitoring, hazardous release notification — and funds lead service line replacement, PFAS treatment, and drinking water system resilience.

Limits methane emissions and flaring from oil and gas operations and counts upstream methane leaks against power plants burning fossil gas, hitting a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide.

analysis.who_pays: Coal and oil-and-gas producers bear the heaviest direct costs: the electricity standard credits generation against an 'efficient coal plant' benchmark that leaves coal with essentially no credit value, methane and flaring rules impose new operating requirements, and fossil generators lose credit value for upstream emissions. Electric utilities must comply with the rising clean-power quota and would likely pass part of the cost to customers' bills, though the bill includes bill-payment assistance and hardship deferrals. Taxpayers fund the grant and rebate programs, which carry open-ended authorizations of appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and gas producers; utilities and their customers

drawbacks.text: The bill lets electricity suppliers buy their way out instead of cutting emissions: suppliers can pay an alternative compliance payment (starting at $40 per credit, rising about 3% a year) or purchase credits in a trading market, so the 100% target can be met on paper through payments rather than direct emission cuts.

Compliance costs under a clean electricity standard would likely show up in electricity bills during the transition; the bill itself acknowledges this by building in a hardship deferral and directing a share of compliance payments to help customers pay their bills.

The bill funds programs that replace natural gas space heaters, water heaters, and stoves with electric appliances, which means upfront replacement costs and consumer pushback in homes that rely on gas.
The bill carries many open-ended authorizations of appropriations for grants, rebates, and federal programs with no stated pay-for, adding to federal spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a serious, detailed attempt at the core policy most climate economists support — a declining cap on power-sector emissions — wrapped in transition help for workers, low-income households, and coal communities, which is the honest answer to the fairness objection. The real weaknesses are the escape valves: compliance payments and credit trading let suppliers delay actual emission cuts, and the spending is unoffset. The costs fall on an identifiable, concentrated set of fossil producers plus some ratepayer pass-through; the benefits are diffuse but large. The bill never got far enough for any of this to be tested in negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to 11 House committees in March 2021; over the remaining 22 months of the Congress only one subcommittee hearing was held, no committee ever voted it out, and it died at the end of the Congress in January 2023 without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: The CLEAN Future Act was introduced on March 2, 2021 by Rep. Frank Pallone with Reps. Tonko and Rush.
The Speaker referred it to 11 committees — Energy and Commerce plus ten others — a referral structure that gives many committees a claim on the bill and makes advancement slow.
It gathered 21 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican signed on.
Between March 2021 and June 2022, the only recorded action beyond referrals was a subcommittee hearing on June 30, 2022.
No committee ever reported the bill to the full House, no floor vote was scheduled, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and electric utilities that faced no new federal clean-electricity mandate, methane limits, or climate disclosure requirements, and retained the regulatory status quo. Ordinary households got none of the bill's efficiency rebates, low-energy-bill assistance, or cleaner air.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and utilities kept the status quo

against.what_they_did: Industry groups broadly opposed economywide clean-electricity mandates, methane restrictions, and fossil-fuel phaseout policies of this kind during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were House Democrats and none was a Republican; the bill never reached a roll-call vote, so no voting split exists beyond the cosponsor record.

industries.note: The clean electricity standard values each plant's output against an 'efficient coal-burning power plant' benchmark, which assigns coal generation essentially no clean-energy credit value, and the bill adds coal ash disposal rules. Coal communities get transition assistance, but the industry's core product is phased out of the electricity standard.

The bill imposes methane and flaring controls, counts upstream oil and gas emissions against power plants burning that fuel, adds hazardous air pollution rules and financial assurance fees, and funds replacement of gas appliances with electric ones. The industry's revenue from electricity and home heating faces direct contraction.

Compliance sits with retail electricity suppliers, who must meet a rising zero-emission quota, but the same structure hands them a new tradable credit market, federal grid modernization funds, and hardship deferrals. Compliance costs would be partly passed to customers, softened by bill-payment assistance drawn from compliance payments.

industries.industry: Renewable energy, nuclear, and storage industries
industries.note: A guaranteed, rising national demand for zero-emission electricity plus tradable credits, solar grants for low-income areas, microgrid funding, and transmission reform create a large, durable market for these industries. Their gains come with the emission cuts the public gets.

Federal grants for domestic EV manufacturing conversion, charging infrastructure buildout, and clean school buses push sales toward electric models, while new greenhouse gas standards for vehicles and engines pressure conventional lines. Manufacturers that convert gain; those that lag lose ground.

The bill creates producer-responsibility standards and plastics reduction programs that impose new costs on packaging and plastics producers, while waste-to-energy facilities qualify for clean-electricity credits and zero-waste grants flow to communities. Gains and losses fall on different parts of the sector.
